There's an old joke that every time Apple unveils a new iPhone Pro, it says it's "the best iPhone we've ever made," as if that statement were somehow surprising.

Specifically, we expect next year to finally move toward that "all-glass" vision, putting a decade of incremental redesigns to rest…

The Evolution of the iPhone Pro Line

If you lined up an iPhone 12 Pro through a 16 Pro, I think most people would struggle to tell them apart at a glance—apart from the shift from the notch to the Dynamic Island in 2022. The iPhone 17 Pro is only barely recognisable, mainly thanks to its elongated camera module and that "cosmic orange" colour.

Of course, each generation brings new features, but to be fair, unless one of them happens to be particularly useful to you, you really need to skip at least two or three generations before it's worth upgrading for a noticeable experience boost.

None of this is meant as a criticism of Apple. The fact is that smartphones are now mature technology, at least in terms of conventional design. You don't see huge differences between adjacent generations because there's genuinely not that much room for improvement year over year.

Apple is now beginning to experiment with different designs—first, of course, with the iPhone Air, and the iPhone Duo—and we expect another major design leap next year, with that 20th-anniversary model.

It's still a little unclear how Apple will position next year's design. Earlier rumours suggested it would be a standalone model, separate from the iPhone 19 Pro line, but other reports say it will be next year's Pro model. There's also the question of whether Apple will use consecutive numbering, or skip a number to mark the milestone—so it might end up being called the iPhone 20 Pro.

For my part, I'd expect it to be the new iPhone Pro design, regardless of whether Apple calls it the 19 or the 20. If so, the iPhone 18 Pro would be the final iteration of this six- or seven-year-old look.

I'll be skipping two generations from the iPhone 16 Pro, so I'll list what each year's model offers me separately. I'll skip the improvements that don't matter to me at all or that I have no use for, like going from a 6-core GPU to a 7-core GPU, and GenLock.

Features Carried Over from the iPhone 17 Pro

  • Center Stage front-facing camera (photos and video calls)
  • Ultra-stabilised video
  • Dual-camera simultaneous recording
  • Telephoto lens upgrade from 5x to 8x
  • Telephoto sensor upgrade from 12MP to 48MP
  • ProRes RAW video
  • Longer battery life
  • Faster charging

What's New on the iPhone 18 Pro

  • Wider maximum aperture on the main lens
  • Variable aperture on the main lens
  • Pro-grade camera controls (aperture, shutter speed, white balance, histogram)
  • Third-generation Photographic Styles
  • Intelligent focus tracking
  • Cinematic effect for standard video
  • Tap-to-zoom and rotate on the front-facing camera
  • Smaller Dynamic Island capable of displaying three Live Activities simultaneously
  • (Even) longer battery life
  • (Even) faster charging

My Personal… Highlights

For me personally, there are five features I'm mainly keeping an eye on at this stage.

Variable aperture lens

While the showstopper is the variable-aperture lens, as I mentioned before, expectations shouldn't be set too high for it. The maximum aperture is only marginally wider, and the sensor is still on the small side, so I'm not expecting a huge difference in shallow depth-of-field effects.

That said, a wider maximum aperture does let in more light—roughly two-thirds of a stop's worth. How much of a difference that makes in practice remains to be seen, but in theory it should translate to shorter exposure times in Night mode. Since I use this feature a lot—usually handheld too—I'm really looking forward to trying it out.

Pro-grade camera controls

Being able to control shutter speed will definitely come in handy when shooting those follow-the-subject-style shots. Full white balance control will also be very useful. And I expect the histogram will be extremely handy when manually adjusting exposure.

I'm generally not a huge fan of filters, whether applied at capture time or tweaked afterwards on the iPhone—I prefer the traditional way of adjusting things. So I rarely use the existing Photographic Styles, and I'm not expecting to use this latest version much more either. But I have to admit, its film presets really appeal to me, so I'll definitely go and try them.

One of the biggest weaknesses of autofocus while filming is that when the subject is briefly obscured by another object, the camera may shift focus to that obstruction. Intelligent focus tracking claims to address exactly this, so I'll definitely be putting it through its paces.

Cinematic Effect for Standard Video

The most upvoted comment came from atonaldenim

I'm really looking forward to hearing your views after you've spent some time with the 18 Pro. I should probably upgrade myself—I'm still on the 12 Mini. (Mini, rest in peace.)

The telephoto lens is going to be a surprise; it might just get me to accept a phone that's so much heavier and bigger than the Mini. I'm currently weighing up whether to pay the full $1,200 for a new 18 Pro, or grab a used 16 Pro for around $700 or less—which seems to be roughly where second-hand prices are right now.

(Pricing between the 17 Pro and 18 Pro is still very close, so I'm not considering the 17 Pro—I'd rather pay a bit more and go straight for the 18 Pro.)

So if you feel the 18 Pro offers a significant step up over the 16 Pro in the areas you mentioned, I'd really like to hear your thoughts. Thanks!

I said less than two months ago that Apple appeared to have given up on Cinematic video mode. I noted at the time that it was a shame, because if Cinematic video were done well, it would be a killer feature for anyone wanting to use an iPhone as a more serious filmmaking tool. To date, it's been almost there, but always missing something; it was always just a little bit off.

Turns out I was wrong: one of the new features of the iPhone 18 is the ability to apply the Cinematic video effect to standard-mode video.

The convenience of not having to decide in advance whether or not to use the mode is welcome, but what interests me most is that Apple appears to be reinvesting in getting the feature right. Meaning they've put the work in, so you can expect it to keep improving, much like Portrait mode did in its early days. I can't wait to try it.

These are the features I feel will make the biggest difference to me personally. How about you? If you've already upgraded to the iPhone 18 Pro, which features drove that decision? Feel free to share in the comments.
